chunks.title: During an earthquake: drop, cover and hold
chunks.text: When you feel strong shaking, protect yourself right away: drop to the ground, take cover (for example under a sturdy table) and hold on until the shaking stops. This is the "drop, cover and hold" that PHIVOLCS asks everyone to do during a strongly felt earthquake.

chunks.title: After an earthquake: aftershocks and damaged buildings
chunks.text: Expect aftershocks for several days to weeks after a strong earthquake. Be careful around buildings that look damaged, because aftershocks can weaken them further. Ask your city or municipal engineering office to inspect a damaged building, and do not go back inside until a structural engineer says it is safe. Check slopes near your home for new cracks: cracked slopes can slide, especially during heavy rain or aftershocks, so stay away from them. Get information only from PHIVOLCS and your local DRRM office, and do not share messages from unconfirmed sources.

chunks.title: Preparing your home for earthquakes
chunks.text: Prepare before an earthquake happens. Fasten heavy furniture and appliances to the walls, and secure hanging objects so they cannot fall on anyone during shaking. Practice drop, cover and hold with your family.

chunks.title: Tsunami warning signs: shake, drop, roar
chunks.text: A tsunami caused by a nearby earthquake can reach the coast within minutes, before any official warning. Learn the three natural signs: strong ground shaking (shake), a sudden drop or change in the sea level (drop), and a roaring sound of incoming waves (roar). If you notice any one of these near the coast, move to high ground immediately and stay away from beaches, rivers and other waterways. After a strong earthquake nearby, stay alert and keep away from the shore.

chunks.title: Earthquake intensity: what the numbers mean
chunks.text: PHIVOLCS reports how strongly an earthquake was felt in each place using the PHIVOLCS Earthquake Intensity Scale (PEIS), from I to X. Intensity I to III: felt by few or many people indoors, with hanging objects swinging. Intensity IV (moderately strong): most people indoors feel it and dishes and windows rattle. Intensity V (strong): most people feel it and some run outdoors. Intensity VI (very strong): many people are frightened, some lose their balance and weak buildings get slight damage. Intensity VII (destructive): people struggle to stand on upper floors and weak or poorly built structures are badly damaged. Intensity VIII to X (very destructive to completely devastating): people cannot stand even outdoors, many or most buildings are damaged or destroyed, and landslides and ground cracks occur.

chunks.title: Before helping anyone
chunks.text: Check that the area is safe for you before approaching an injured person. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) for serious injuries. Wear gloves or use a plastic bag as a barrier if available when touching blood.

chunks.title: Bleeding
chunks.text: Stop bleeding by pressing firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth, gauze or bandage, and keep pressing. Wear gloves or clean your hands first if you can. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top instead of removing the first layer. Go to a health facility if the wound is deep or large, if the bleeding does not stop, or if it is a puncture wound such as from a nail.

chunks.title: Cuts and wounds
chunks.text: Once a small cut stops bleeding, rinse it under clean running water, wash it with soap and water, and cover it with a clean gauze pad or adhesive bandage. See a health worker if the wound is deep or large, keeps bleeding, or has a high risk of infection, such as a puncture from a nail or a wound from floodwater or an animal bite.

chunks.title: Burns
chunks.text: First stop the burning: move the person away from the heat, or remove the heat source. Cool the burn with cool or cold running water for at least 10 minutes. Do not put ice directly on it, and do not use toothpaste, butter or oil. Do not break blisters. Cover the burn loosely with a clean, sterile dressing. Get medical help if the burn is deep or large; if it is on the hands, feet, face, groin or head; if it goes all the way around an arm or leg; or if it shows signs of infection.

chunks.title: Possible broken bones
chunks.text: Do not try to straighten the injured part. Keep it still with a splint made from a board, rolled newspaper, or cardboard, padded with cloth and tied above and below the injury. Seek medical care.

chunks.title: Dehydration and heat exhaustion
chunks.text: Heat exhaustion can start with tiredness, dizziness, headache, vomiting, weakness or feeling faint. Move the person to a cool, shaded place with good air flow and remove outer clothing. Cool them with cold compresses or cold wet cloths on the head, neck, armpits, wrists, ankles and groin. If they are awake, give frequent small sips of cool water. Heat stroke is an emergency: very high body temperature, a fast heartbeat, confusion, seizures or unconsciousness. Start cooling right away and get the person to a hospital or call 911.

chunks.title: Unresponsive person
chunks.text: If a person does not respond and is not breathing normally, call 911 and start CPR if you are trained: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute. If the person is breathing, turn them on their side in the recovery position and stay with them until help arrives.

chunks.title: Warning signs of flooding
chunks.text: Heavy rain for many hours, rapidly rising rivers or creeks, and water entering streets are signs of possible flooding. Flash floods can arrive within minutes, especially near rivers and in low areas. If authorities issue a flood or rainfall warning for your area, prepare to move to higher ground.

chunks.title: Walking or driving through floodwater
chunks.text: Avoid walking or driving through floodwater. Just 15 centimeters (6 inches) of fast-moving water can knock an adult down, and about 60 centimeters (2 feet) can carry away a car. Floodwater can hide open manholes, sharp debris, and live electrical wires. If you must walk through water, use a stick to check the ground in front of you and walk where the water is not moving.

chunks.title: Electrical safety in floods
chunks.text: Turn off the main power switch before water enters the house, but only if you are standing on dry ground. Never touch electrical appliances, outlets, or switches while you are wet or standing in water. Stay away from fallen power lines and report them.

chunks.title: Health risks after floods
chunks.text: Floodwater can carry leptospirosis, a serious infection from animal urine that enters through cuts and through the eyes, nose or mouth. Avoid wading in floodwater. If you cannot avoid it, wear boots and gloves, and wash your hands, feet and any exposed skin with soap and water afterwards. Symptoms can appear up to about 4 weeks later: high fever, muscle pain, red eyes, chills, severe headache, vomiting, diarrhea or yellowish skin. If you get any of these after being in floodwater, see a doctor right away. A doctor may give a preventive medicine (doxycycline) after wading; it needs a prescription, so do not take it on your own.

chunks.title: Clean drinking water
chunks.text: Do not drink floodwater or water from flooded wells. If you are not sure your water is safe, bring it to a rolling boil for at least 2 minutes, or disinfect it with chlorine, before drinking. Throw away food that touched floodwater.

chunks.title: If you are trapped by rising water
chunks.text: Move to the highest floor or the roof. Do not enter a closed attic without a way out. Signal for help with a whistle, flashlight, or brightly colored cloth. Call emergency services (911 in the Philippines) if you have a signal.

chunks.title: What a go-bag is
chunks.text: A go-bag (emergency bag) is a ready-packed bag you can grab immediately when you must evacuate, with what your family needs for at least 3 days. Keep it where you can reach it quickly and light enough to carry while walking. Check it every three months and replace expired food, water and medicine.

chunks.title: Water and food
chunks.text: Pack bottled drinking water for each person, and ready-to-eat food, for at least 3 days: food that does not need cooking, such as canned goods with pull-tab lids, crackers, biscuits and energy bars. Include a manual can opener if your cans need one.

chunks.title: Documents and money
chunks.text: Put important documents in a sealed, waterproof plastic bag: valid IDs, birth certificates, land titles, insurance papers, and medical records or prescriptions. Bring cash in small bills and coins, because ATMs and card payments may not work during a brownout. Write important phone numbers on paper in case your phone battery dies.

chunks.title: Light, power, and communication
chunks.text: Pack a flashlight, a whistle to signal for help, matches, a portable radio with spare batteries to hear official announcements, and your mobile phone with a charged power bank and cable. If you bring a candle, never leave it burning unattended, especially in crowded evacuation areas.

chunks.title: Medicine and first aid
chunks.text: Pack a first aid kit with bandages, gauze and medicine for fever, diarrhea and wounds. Bring your regular maintenance medicines with a copy of the prescription, plus soap, face masks, and sanitary and personal hygiene items.

chunks.title: Clothes and protection
chunks.text: Pack a change of clothes, rain gear such as a raincoat or poncho, and a blanket or sleeping bag. Sturdy closed shoes or boots help in flooded or damaged areas. A rope can also be useful.

chunks.title: Infants and young children
chunks.text: For infants and babies, bring diapers, wipes, baby formula or breast-milk storage supplies, clean bottles, safe drinking water for mixing formula, extra baby clothes, a blanket and any baby medicines. For young children, bring a familiar small toy or comfort item. Write your contact number on a card in each child's pocket in case you get separated.

chunks.title: Older adults, persons with disabilities, and pets
chunks.text: Add what older adults and persons with disabilities need: extra maintenance medicine, eyeglasses, hearing-aid batteries, mobility aids and adult diapers. Write down medical conditions and doctor contacts. For pets, pack food, water, a leash or carrier and vaccination records, and ask in advance whether your evacuation site accepts pets.

chunks.title: National emergency hotline 911
chunks.text: The number to call in an emergency is 911. For any emergency anywhere in the Philippines (police, fire, medical, rescue), call 911. It is the national emergency hotline, free and open 24 hours. It replaced the PNP Patrol 117 line, and since September 2025 the DILG's unified 911 also takes the place of many local emergency numbers.

chunks.title: Other towns and barangays
chunks.text: For other municipalities in the map area (for example Tanauan, Santo Tomas, Bauan, San Pascual, Ibaan, Rosario, San Jose, Cuenca, Mabini, Taal, Malvar and Tingloy), this device has no verified hotline list yet. Call 911, the Batangas PDRRMO, or your municipal hall. Your barangay hall and its Barangay DRRM Committee are usually the first responders for evacuation. Facility records on the map sometimes include a phone number from OpenStreetMap; treat those as unverified.

chunks.title: Preparing for brownouts
chunks.text: Keep flashlights and spare batteries where everyone can find them in the dark. Keep phones and power banks charged when power is available. Know how to reach your electric cooperative or utility to report outages.

chunks.title: Lighting safely
chunks.text: Flashlights and battery LED lamps are safer than candles or kerosene lamps. If you must use a candle or oil lamp, put it in a proper, stable holder, away from curtains and where children or pets cannot knock it over. Never leave it burning unattended, and put it out before you sleep.

chunks.title: Generators and carbon monoxide
chunks.text: A generator used the wrong way can fill a house, garage or building with carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never run a generator indoors or in a closed garage; keep it outdoors and away from windows and doors. Signs of carbon monoxide poisoning include headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, shortness of breath and feeling weak or sick: move to fresh air immediately and seek medical help.
chunks.source: Department of Health (via Philippine News Agency)

chunks.title: Appliances and power surges
chunks.text: Unplug appliances you are not using, especially during an outage, so they are not damaged when power comes back. Do not overload outlets or extension cords, and replace frayed cords right away. Leave one light switched on so you know when the power is back.
chunks.source: Bureau of Fire Protection (via Philippine Information Agency)

chunks.title: Food safety without refrigeration
chunks.text: Keep the refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible. A closed refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours. Throw away perishable food such as meat, fish, eggs, and leftovers that have been above refrigerator temperature for more than 2 hours or that smell or look unusual.

chunks.title: Saving phone battery
chunks.text: Lower screen brightness, turn on battery saver, close unused apps, and turn off mobile data and Wi-Fi when you do not need them. Send text messages instead of calling when networks are congested, because texts need less network capacity.

chunks.title: Heat during outages
chunks.text: Without fans or air conditioning, drink plenty of water and avoid soda, coffee, iced tea and alcohol. Wear loose, light clothing, stay in the coolest shaded part of the house, and limit time outdoors between 10 am and 4 pm. Check on infants, young children, older adults and sick people, who are more affected by heat.

chunks.title: Taal Volcano alert levels 0 to 2
chunks.text: PHIVOLCS uses alert levels 0 to 5 for Taal Volcano. Alert Level 0 (normal): no major eruption is expected, but steam and gas explosions can still happen without warning, and no one should live permanently on Taal Volcano Island. Alert Level 1 (low-level unrest): steam or gas explosions can happen without warning; entry into the Main Crater, the Daang Kastila fissure area and the Mt. Tabaro eruption site is not allowed. Alert Level 2 (increasing unrest): explosions are more likely; entry into Taal Volcano Island is not allowed, and communities in the highest-hazard areas must prepare for possible evacuation. Saved information on this device cannot tell you the current alert level: follow PHIVOLCS and your municipal DRRM office.

chunks.title: Taal Volcano alert levels 3 to 5: evacuation
chunks.text: Alert Level 3 (magmatic unrest): an eruption is imminent; Taal Volcano Island, Taal Lake and the pre-identified Batangas lakeshore communities facing the active vent must be evacuated. Alert Level 4 (hazardous eruption imminent): a strong eruption is underway and could become violently explosive; communities in the pre-determined hazard zones must be evacuated. Alert Level 5 (highly hazardous eruption in progress): a violent eruption is ongoing, and more areas may need to evacuate depending on conditions. If you live in these areas, follow your local government's evacuation orders.

chunks.title: Dangers during a Taal eruption
chunks.text: A violent eruption of Taal can bring base surges and pyroclastic density currents (fast, hot clouds of gas and rock that sweep across the lake and land), a volcanic tsunami on Taal Lake, thick ashfall, ground cracks, lahars (volcanic mudflows) and landslides. These are why PHIVOLCS asks people to leave the island, the lake and the lakeshore when the alert level rises.

chunks.title: Ashfall: protecting your health
chunks.text: During ashfall, stay indoors and limit outdoor activities. Close windows and doors, and turn off air conditioners and fans so ash does not get inside. If you must go out, wear an N95 mask, protective clothing and goggles. People with asthma or other breathing problems should use an N95 mask; others may use a dust or surgical mask. Ash can irritate the nose, throat and eyes and cause coughing or difficult breathing: anyone with these symptoms should go to the nearest health facility.

chunks.title: Ashfall on the skin
chunks.text: Cover your skin when you go out during ashfall. If ash gets on your skin, wash it off promptly with clean water and mild soap, and do not scratch itchy skin.

chunks.title: Before typhoon season
chunks.text: Know your area's hazards: flooding, landslides, and storm surge along the coast. Find out where your barangay's designated evacuation center is and walk the route in daylight. Prepare a go-bag for each family member and agree on a family meeting place and a contact person outside your area.
chunks.source: Senate Committee on Climate Change with NDRRMC and PAGASA (2011 handbook)

chunks.title: Understanding warnings
chunks.text: PAGASA issues Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals (TCWS) numbered 1 to 5 for specific areas. A higher number means stronger winds and less warning time. Signal No. 1: winds of 39 to 61 km/h expected within 36 hours, minimal to minor threat to lives and properties. Signal No. 2: 62 to 88 km/h within 24 hours, minor to moderate threat. Signal No. 3: 89 to 117 km/h within 18 hours, moderate to significant threat. Signal No. 4: 118 to 184 km/h within 12 hours, significant to severe threat. Signal No. 5: 185 km/h or higher within 12 hours, extreme threat to lives and properties. (Source: DOST-PAGASA press release on the modified TCWS system, 23 March 2022.) Listen for whether your province or municipality is included, and follow PAGASA, NDRRMC, and your local government on radio or TV. Saved information on this device cannot tell you the current signal level.

chunks.title: When a typhoon is approaching
chunks.text: Charge phones and power banks, fill containers with clean water, and stock food that does not need cooking. Secure or bring inside loose objects that strong winds can throw, such as roofing sheets, plants, and signs. Trim weak tree branches near the house if it is safe to do so. Move important items and electrical appliances to higher shelves in case of flooding.
chunks.source: Senate Committee on Climate Change with NDRRMC and PAGASA (2011 handbook)

chunks.title: When to evacuate
chunks.text: Evacuate immediately when local authorities order it, especially if you live in a low-lying, coastal, riverside, or landslide-prone area. Do not wait for water to rise. Bring your go-bag, turn off the main power switch and gas if you can do so safely, and lock your house.
chunks.source: Senate Committee on Climate Change with NDRRMC and PAGASA (2011 handbook)

chunks.title: During the typhoon
chunks.text: Stay indoors and away from windows and glass doors. Stay in the strongest part of the house. Do not go outside during the calm "eye" of the storm: after about one to two hours the worst winds return suddenly from the opposite direction. Keep listening to a battery-powered radio for updates.
chunks.source: Senate Committee on Climate Change with NDRRMC and PAGASA (2011 handbook)

chunks.title: After the typhoon
chunks.text: Wait for authorities to say it is safe before returning home. Watch for fallen power lines, damaged structures, and floodwater. Do not touch electrical lines. Check your house for damage before entering. Boil drinking water or use treated water if the supply may be contaminated.
